paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Seafloor spreading is a process that happens at mid-ocean ridges. Volcanic activity there makes new oceanic crust, and that crust then slowly moves away from the ridge. It happens where two plates move apart. The sites are called spreading centers, and hydrothermal vents are common at them.

paragraphs.heading: The idea it replaced
paragraphs.text: Earlier theories of continental drift, from Alfred Wegener and Alexander du Toit, held that moving continents plowed through a seafloor that stayed fixed. Robert Dietz, of the U.S. Naval Electronics Laboratory in San Diego, and Harold Hammond Hess, of Princeton University, proposed something different in the 1960s. They said the seafloor itself moves, spreading from a central rift axis and carrying the continents with it. Today the phenomenon is known as plate tectonics, and seafloor spreading helps explain continental drift within that theory.

paragraphs.heading: How it works
paragraphs.text: When oceanic plates pull apart, tensional stress fractures the lithosphere. Basaltic magma rises up those fractures and cools on the ocean floor, forming new seabed. Younger rocks are found nearer the spreading zone and older rocks farther from it. The motivating force is not magma pressure, though there is typically a lot of magma activity at spreading ridges. It is slab pull, the pull of tectonic plates at subduction zones. Plates can also be driven by ridge push, in which the rigid lithosphere slides down the raised, hot asthenosphere that lies below mid-ocean ridges.

paragraphs.heading: Fast and slow ridges
paragraphs.text: The spreading rate is how quickly an ocean basin widens because of seafloor spreading. Each plate on either side of the ridge gains new lithosphere at half that rate, called the spreading half-rate. Ridges are sorted by rate into fast, intermediate and slow. As a general rule, fast ridges open at more than 90 mm/year, intermediate ridges at 40–90 mm/year, and slow ridges at less than 40 mm/year. The highest rate known, over 200 mm/yr, was on the East Pacific Rise during the Miocene.

paragraphs.heading: Magnetic stripes as a clock
paragraphs.text: In the 1960s, magnetic stripes on the ocean floor revealed the past record of reversals of Earth's magnetic field. The stripes can be read by towing a magnetometer along the sea surface or flying one on an aircraft, and the polarity of the past field can be inferred from them. The stripes on one side of a mid-ocean ridge mirrored those on the other. Scientists could identify a reversal of known age, measure how far it lay from the spreading center, and compute the spreading half-rate. In some places the half-rates on the two sides of the ridge crest differ by about five percent. This is thought to come from temperature gradients in the asthenosphere caused by mantle plumes near the spreading center.

paragraphs.heading: How spreading begins
paragraphs.text: In the general case, seafloor spreading begins as a rift in a continental land mass, much like the Red Sea-East Africa Rift System today. Heating at the base of the continental crust makes it more plastic and less dense. Less dense material rises relative to denser material, so the heated area swells into a broad dome. As the crust bows upward it fractures, and the fractures slowly grow into rifts. A typical rift system has three arms at roughly 120-degree angles. If spreading goes on, two arms open while the third stops opening and becomes a failed rift, or aulacogen.

paragraphs.heading: A new sea
paragraphs.text: As the two active rifts keep opening, the continental crust is eventually stretched as far as it will go. Basaltic oceanic crust and upper mantle lithosphere then start to form between the separating pieces of continent. When one rift opens into an existing ocean, seawater floods the rift system and it becomes a new sea; the Red Sea is an example. The new sea evaporates, partly or completely, several times before the rift valley's elevation has been lowered enough for the sea to become stable. During this evaporation, large evaporite deposits are laid down in the rift valley.
